title: Did Your Phone Just Buzz?
passage: Have you ever felt your phone vibrate in your pocket, checked it, and found no new messages? If so, you're not alone. Scientists call this 'phantom vibration syndrome', and some studies suggest that up to 90% of phone users have experienced it. Why does it happen? Our brains are constantly trying to predict what is going on around us. If you're waiting for an important message, your brain becomes extra sensitive, so it may 'translate' a small movement of your clothes into a vibration. In other words, your brain would rather make a mistake than miss something important. Is it dangerous? Not really — experts say it's a normal reaction, not an illness. However, if it happens very often, it might be a sign that you're thinking about your phone too much. One simple solution is to switch notifications off for a few hours a day. Your brain will thank you.

title: Should Schools Ban Phones?
passage: More and more schools around the world are banning phones during the school day, and the debate about whether this is a good idea is getting louder. Supporters of the bans argue that phones are a constant distraction. Even when a phone is switched off, they say, just having it on your desk makes it harder to concentrate. Some schools that introduced bans have reported that students talk to each other more at break and that cases of online bullying during school hours have dropped. However, not everyone is convinced. Critics point out that phones can be useful learning tools — for looking up information, recording homework or using educational apps. Many parents also want to be able to contact their children in an emergency. And some students argue that banning phones doesn't teach young people how to manage their screen time; it simply moves the problem to after school. Perhaps the answer lies somewhere in the middle. A number of schools now allow phones only for specific tasks in class, while keeping them in lockers the rest of the time. Whether this compromise works, only time will tell.

title: Why Losing Was the Best Thing That Happened to Me
passage: Last spring I entered my first national coding competition. I'd been teaching myself to code for two years, mostly by watching tutorials late at night, and I was secretly convinced I would win. I didn't. In fact, I came 47th out of 60. For about a week I was too embarrassed to open my laptop. What made it worse was that my app had crashed in the middle of my presentation, in front of the judges and about a hundred people. Then one of the judges emailed me. I assumed she was going to tell me politely that coding wasn't for me. Instead, she said my idea — an app that helps students share notes — was one of the most original in the competition, and that the crash was 'the kind of thing that happens to every developer, usually at the worst possible moment'. She even sent me a list of things to improve. I spent the summer rebuilding the app from scratch, this time testing it properly. It now has a few hundred users at my school. I still haven't won a competition, but I've stopped being afraid of failing in public, and that feels like a bigger prize.

title: The Lost Laboratory — escape room review
passage: For my friend's birthday, five of us tried The Lost Laboratory, the newest escape room in town. The idea is that you're trapped in the lab of a scientist who disappeared in the middle of an experiment, and you have sixty minutes to find out what happened and get out before the 'experiment' destroys the building. First, the positives. The room itself is incredibly detailed: there are bubbling test tubes, a flickering computer screen and a creepy voice that gives you clues if you get stuck. The puzzles are clever and varied — some involve maths, others observation or teamwork — so everyone in our group had a chance to shine. The staff were friendly and clearly loved their job. That said, it's not perfect. A couple of puzzles depend on finding tiny objects in dark corners, which felt more frustrating than challenging. It's also quite pricey if you go as a small group, since you pay per room rather than per person. Overall, though, we had a brilliant time and escaped with just forty seconds to spare. I'd recommend it to groups of four to six who enjoy a challenge — but maybe not to anyone who's scared of the dark.

topic_en: Article: songs stuck in your head
title: Can't Get It Out of Your Head?
passage: You hear a few seconds of a song in a shop, and for the rest of the day it plays in your head on repeat. Psychologists call these tunes 'earworms', and studies suggest that around 90% of people experience them at least once a week. So why do some songs stick while others don't? Research shows that earworms tend to have a few things in common: they are usually fairly fast, they have a simple melody that is easy to sing, and they contain an unexpected jump or repetition that our brains find surprising. Interestingly, the songs don't have to be ones we like — many people report being 'infected' by tunes they actively dislike. Earworms are also more likely to appear when our minds are not fully occupied, for example when we are walking or doing the washing-up. So how can you get rid of one? Surprisingly, one of the most effective methods is to listen to the whole song from beginning to end. Scientists believe that our brains keep replaying a tune partly because it feels unfinished. Another option is to give your brain a moderately difficult task, such as a puzzle. Chewing gum may also help, as it makes it harder to 'sing' silently in your head.
